module.title: Python for dependable data work
module.summary: Read CSV and JSON records into typed Python values under a written contract, keep every refusal with its reason, and make the program explain itself with tracebacks, logs, assertions and tests in a recorded, pinned environment.
objectives: Predict the type and value csv and json hand you, and keep missing, null, blank and zero apart.
Write conversion functions that refuse what int(), Decimal() and date.fromisoformat() accept, and land every record once with a named reason.
Read a traceback to its failing line and input, and use exceptions, assertions, logging and type hints for their actual jobs.
Prove behaviour with unittest tests against hand-written literals in a recorded, pinned environment.

scenarios.title: Explain Cinderline's reconciled inspection counts to quality engineering
scenarios.context: Fictional Cinderline Components compares defect rates by plant each week. Plant CL-N sends CSV and plant CL-S sends JSON. Last week a notebook converted every value with int() and float() inside a try/except that skipped any row that raised, and reported totals neither plant recognised. The lab's parser now reports 7 accepted and 18 rejected records from 25 received. The quality lead wants to know which numbers to trust, why records were refused and what is still open.
scenarios.task: Write the note that goes with the parsed delivery: what was accepted and rejected and why, how the counts reconcile, what the old notebook got wrong, what was tested and in which environment, and what remains unknown.
requirements: Reconcile received, accepted and rejected counts per source and name every rejection reason with its count.
Explain at least three silent errors of the old int()/float() approach using specific records.
Keep code invariants (assertions), data rules (validation) and diagnostics (logs, tracebacks) apart in the explanation.
State the environment and tests behind the result, and list open questions for the plants instead of guessing.
scenarios.model:
### Counts
25 records received: 15 from CL-N (CSV) and 10 from CL-S (JSON). 7 accepted (3 CSV, 4 JSON) and 18 rejected, so 7 + 18 = 25; the parser asserts this on every run. Nineteen reasons over 18 records, because CLN-015 carries two.

### Why records were refused
Malformed quantities (4: 'twelve', '12.0', 12.5 and true), malformed dates (2: '2026/09/03' and '2026-09-31'), one malformed cost ('4,25'), missing values (4), one null quantity, three negative values (negative_inspected_units on CLN-005 and CLN-015, negative_defective_units on CLN-015), one record with 45 defective of 40, one exact repeat of CLN-001 and one conflicting pair, CLN-008 with 15 against 16 inspected.

### What the old notebook did
It counted CLS-006's true as 1 unit and CLS-005's 12.5 as 12, summed CLN-001 twice and both conflicting CLN-008 counts, added CLN-005's and CLN-015's negative quantities, and skipped 'twelve' without saying so. None of these raised an error that anyone saw, and the skipped rows left no trace of why the totals shrank.

### Evidence
36 unit tests against hand-written literals pass on CPython 3.12.3 with the standard library only, zero skipped; the evidence file records the interpreter and SHA-256 hashes of fixtures and outputs. Rejected records keep their raw values, and every rejection is logged.

### Open questions
CL-S: does a null quantity mean 'not inspected' or 'unknown'? CL-N: which CLN-008 count is right? Until they answer, those records stay rejected and listed with their raw values.
scenarios.reasoning: The note leads with a reconciliation the reader can check, attributes each old error to a specific record and mechanism, keeps the assertion, the validation rules and the logs in their own roles, and turns ambiguity into named questions for the data owners instead of a silent default.

rubric.partial: Gives totals but not per source or not per reason.
rubric.strong: States 25 = 7 + 18 per source, 19 reasons by kind, and names the assertion that guards it.

rubric.weak: Says the old numbers were wrong without specifics.
rubric.partial: Names int() or duplicates in general terms.
rubric.strong: Names specific records (true as 1, 12.5 as 12, CLN-001 twice, 'twelve' skipped) and the mechanism behind each.

rubric.weak: Treats logs, asserts and validation as interchangeable.
rubric.partial: Separates validation from logging but not from assertions.
rubric.strong: Validation produces reasons, the assertion guards the code's bookkeeping, logs and tracebacks diagnose.

rubric.partial: Mentions tests without the environment or the open questions.
rubric.strong: Names tests, literals and interpreter, lists what is unknown and routes it to the plants.

disclosures.question: Can null quantities simply be treated as zero so the totals look complete?
disclosures.response: Not yet. CL-S's data contact says null is sometimes sent when a tally sheet was not returned, so zero would publish a measurement nobody took. They will confirm the meaning next week.

disclosures.question: Which CLN-008 count is right, 15 or 16?
disclosures.response: CL-N's supervisor believes 16 is a recount but cannot find the tally sheet; both records stay rejected as conflicting until it is found.

claims.description: Python compares by type and never casts text to a number in a comparison, so '12' == 12 is False; bool subclasses int; floats are binary approximations; None, False, 0 and '' are false in a truth test.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: A dict maps unique hashable keys to values, a list is ordered and mutable, a tuple is immutable, a set holds distinct hashable members, and comprehensions build these collections from for and if clauses.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: int() accepts whitespace, a sign and underscores, truncates floats and accepts bool; Decimal built from a float converts its exact binary value and an invalid string signals InvalidOperation; date.fromisoformat accepts forms such as 20260903 only since Python 3.11.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: csv.DictReader returns dicts of strings keyed by the header; json.load maps null to None, true to True and numbers to int or float; with blocks close files even when an exception is raised.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: A traceback lists the most recent call last and ends with the exception type and message; ValueError, TypeError and KeyError mark a bad value, a bad type and a missing key; assert statements generate no code under python -O.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: logging.getLogger(name) returns one shared logger per dotted name; basicConfig configures the root logger; libraries should add no handler other than NullHandler.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: Importing a module runs its top level once per session; a module run as a script has __name__ '__main__', so a guarded block runs only then.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: unittest tests are TestCase methods named test… that use assertion methods such as assertEqual and assertLogs; assertLogs reports LEVEL:logger:message lines.
claims.context: CPython 3.12; other versions noted where they differ.

claims.description: The runtime does not enforce type annotations; X | Y union syntax is available from Python 3.10.

concepts.definition: The class of a Python value, such as str, int, float, bool or NoneType, which decides how it compares and converts.
A mutable mapping from unique hashable keys to values, the Python shape of one record keyed by column name.
Ordered mutable sequences, immutable groups and unordered collections of distinct hashable values.
Python's single object for an explicit absence of a value, distinct from an absent key, an empty string and zero.
A function that returns one type for the inputs a contract allows and raises ValueError for everything else.
An exact decimal number type that keeps the digits and scale it was built from, used for money instead of binary float.
Standard-library functions that turn file text into dicts of strings (DictReader) or typed values with null as None (json.load).
A refused record kept with its source, position, untouched raw input and reasons instead of being dropped.
An expression that builds a list, set or dict from a for clause and optional if clauses.
The printed call stack of an unhandled exception, most recent call last, ending with the exception type and message.
An except clause that catches named exception types raised in its try block and decides what happens instead.
A statement that raises AssertionError when its expression is false and generates no code under python -O.
A named, hierarchical logging channel whose destinations are chosen by the application's handlers.
A Python file whose top level runs once on import, with script-only work under a check that __name__ equals '__main__'.
An annotation describing expected types for readers and static tools, which the Python runtime does not enforce.
A small automated check that compares code output with an independently written expectation.
A directory created by python -m venv with its own site-packages on top of a base interpreter.
